solution: Solution: For $0 < x < 1$ , $I = \int [\tan^{-1}(1-x+x^2) + \tan^{-1}(1-x)] \, dx$ $= \int \tan^{-1} \left[ \frac{(1-x+x^2)+(1-x)}{1-(1-x+x^2)(1-x)} \right] dx$ $= \int \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{2-2x+x^2}{x(2-2x+x^2)} \right) dx$ $= \int \tan^{-1} \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) dx$ $= \int \cot^{-1}(x) \, dx = \int \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1} x \right) dx$ $= \int \frac{\pi}{2} \, dx - \int \tan^{-1} x \, dx$ $= \frac{\pi}{2} x - \left[ x \tan^{-1} x - \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C \right]$ [Using product rule] $= \frac{\pi}{2} x - x \tan^{-1} x + \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C$ where $C =$ constant of integration $= x \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1} x \right) + \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C$ $= x \cot^{-1} x + \frac{1}{2} \ln (1+x^2) + C$ $= x \cot^{-1} x + \log \sqrt{1+x^2} + C$ © examsnet.com

question: $\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(2x) \cos^6(2x) dx=$ [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: $I=\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(2x) \cos^6(2x) dx$ Let $u=2x$ , then $du=2dx$ , so $dx=\frac{1}{2} du$ When $x=-2\pi, u=2(-2\pi)=-4\pi$ when $x=2\pi, u=2(2\pi)=4\pi$ $I=\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(2x) \cos^6(2x) dx$ $=\frac{1}{2} \int\limits_{-4\pi}^{4\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ Since, $\sin(u)$ and $\cos(u)$ are periodic with a period of $2\pi$ , So, $\sin^4(u)$ and $\cos^6(u)$ are also periodic with a period of $2\pi$ $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=\int\limits_{-2\pi}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 4 \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=2 \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ Since, the function, $f(u)=\sin^4(u) \cos^6(u)$ is an even function. $\therefore 2 \int\limits_{0}^{2\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=2 \cdot 2 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=4 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=4 \cdot 2 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=8 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ We know that, $\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^m(u) \cos^n(u) du$ $=\frac{(m-1)(m-3)\dots (1\ \text{or}\ 2)(n-1)(n-3)\dots (1\ \text{or}\ 2)}{(m+n)(m+n-2)\dots (1\ \text{or}\ 2)} \times \alpha$ where, $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}$ if both $m$ and $n$ are even, and $\alpha=1$ otherness. Here, $m=4, n=6$ both are even. So, $\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(4) \cos^6(4) du$ $=\frac{(4-1)(4-3)(6-1)(6-3)(6-5)}{(4+6)(4+6-2)(4+6-4)} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}$ $(4+6-6)(4+6-8)$ $=\frac{3 \cdot 1 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 \cdot 1}{10 \cdot 8 \cdot 6 \cdot 4 \cdot 2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{45}{3840} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{3}{256} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2}$ $=\frac{3\pi}{512}$ $\therefore 8 \int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du$ $=8 \cdot \frac{3\pi}{512} = \frac{24\pi}{512} = \frac{3\pi}{64}$ $\therefore 8 \int\limits_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin^4(u) \cos^6(u) du = \frac{3\pi}{64}$ © examsnet.com

question: If $f(t)=\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx, n\in N$ , then $f(t+\pi)=$ [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, $f(t)=\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx, n\in$ So, $f(t+\pi)=\int\limits_{0}^{t+\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx$ $=\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx+\int\limits_{t}^{t+\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)} x\,dx$ Let $u=x-\pi$ $\Rightarrow du=dx$ Limit, when $x=t, u=t-\pi$ and $x=t+\pi, u=t$ So, $f(t+\pi)=f(t)+\int\limits_{t}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u+\pi)\,du$ Since, $\tan(u+\pi)=\tan u$ $\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{t-\pi}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1}(u)\,du$ $\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{t-\pi}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du+\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du$ Let $v=-u$ , the $dv=-du$ When $u=t-\pi, v=\pi-t$ , when $u=0, v=0$ , so we get $\;=f(t)-\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(-v)\,dv+\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du$ $\;\;\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv+\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(u)\,du$ $\;=f(t)+\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv+f(t)$ $\;=2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi-t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv$ $\;=2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{\pi-t}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv$ Let $w=v-\pi$ , then $dw=dv$ When $v=\pi-t, w=-t$ , when $v=\pi$ $w=0$ $\;=2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(w+\pi)\,dw$ $\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{-t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(w)\,dw$ Let $z=-w$ , then $dz=-dw$ when $w=-t, z=t$ and $w=0, z=0$ $=\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv+\int\limits_{t}^{0} \tan^{(2n-1)}(-z)\,dz$ $=\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-\int\limits_{0}^{t} \tan^{(2n-1)}(z)\,dz$ $=\;2f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv-f(t)$ $=\;f(t)-\int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv$ $=\;f(t)+0 \left[ \because \int\limits_{0}^{\pi} \tan^{(2n-1)}(v)\,dv=0 \right]$ $\;=f(t)+f(\pi) \;\; [ \because f(\pi)=0 ]$ $\therefore \;f(t+\pi)=f(t)+f(\pi)$ © examsnet.com

question: $\int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx =$ [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: $I = \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4-x^2}{x^2} \right)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \cdot \frac{(4-x^2)^{5/2}}{x^5} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^3 (4-x^2)^{5/2} dx$ Let $u = 4 - x^2$ Then, $du = -2x \, dx$ , so $x \, dx = -\frac{1}{2} du \quad x^2 = 4 - u$ and $x^3 = x \cdot x^2 = x(4-u)$ when $x = 0, \quad u = 4$ and when $x = 2, \quad u = 0$ $\therefore \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^3 (4-x^2)^{5/2} dx$ $= \int\limits_{4}^{0(4-u)} \cdot u^{5/2} \cdot \left( -\frac{1}{2} \right) du$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ 4 \cdot \frac{u^{7/2}}{7/2} - \frac{u^{9/2}}{9/2} \right]_{0}^{4}$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{8}{7} u^{7/2} - \frac{2}{9} u^{9/2} \right]_{0}^{4}$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{8}{7} (u)^{7/2} - \frac{2}{9} (4)^{9/2} - 0 \right]$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{8}{7} (128) - \frac{2}{9} (512) \right]$ $= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{1024}{7} - \frac{1024}{9} \right]$ $= \frac{1024}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{63} = \frac{1024}{63}$ $\therefore \int\limits_{0}^{2} x^8 \left( \frac{4}{x^2} - 1 \right)^{5/2} dx = \frac{1024}{63} = \frac{2^{10}}{63}$ © examsnet.com

question: The area (in sq.units) of the region bounded by the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=8-x^2$ is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, curves are $y=x^2$ and $y=8-x^2$ Equating these two equations, we get $\;x^2=8-x^2 \Rightarrow 2 x^2=8$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\; x^2=4 \Rightarrow x= \pm 2$ $\;\;\text{ Thus, area }\;=\int\limits_{-2}^{2} [ (8-x^2) -x^2] dx$ $\; \;\;\;\;  \;=\int\limits_{-2}^{2} (8-x^2-x^2) dx=\int\limits_{-2}^{2} (8-2 x^2) dx$ $\;= \left[8 x-\;\frac{2}{3} x^3\right]_{-2}^2$ $\;= \{8(2)-\;\frac{2}{3}(2)^3\} - \{8(-2)-\;\frac{2}{3}(-2)^3\}$ $\;= \left(16-\;\frac{16}{3}\right) - \left(-16+\;\frac{16}{3}\right)$ $\;=16-\;\frac{16}{3}+16-\;\frac{16}{3}$ $\;=32-\;\frac{32}{3}=\;\frac{96-32}{3}=\;\frac{64}{3}$ ∴ The area of the region bounded by the curves is $\;\frac{64}{3}$ sq. units. © examsnet.com

question: The solution of the differential equation $x^2(y+1) \frac{dy}{dx} + y^2(x+1)^2 = 0$ , when $y(1)=2$ , is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, differential equation is $x^2(y+1) \frac{dy}{dx} + y^2(x+1)^2 = 0, y(1)=2$ $\Rightarrow x^2(y+1) \frac{dy}{dx} = -y^2(x+1)^2$ $\Rightarrow \frac{y+1}{y^2} dy = -\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2} dx$ Integrating to both sides, we get $\int \frac{y+1}{y^2} dy = -\int \frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2} dx$ $\Rightarrow \int \left( \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{y^2} \right) dy$ $= -\int \left( 1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{1}{x^2} \right) dx$ $\Rightarrow \ln|y| - \frac{1}{y} = -\left( x + 2\ln|x| - \frac{1}{x} \right) + C,$ where $C=$ constant $\Rightarrow \ln|y| + 2\ln|x| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x + C$ $\Rightarrow \ln|x^2 y| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x + C \cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot\cdot \text{(i)}$ Given, $y(1)=2$ , so we get $\Rightarrow \ln|1^2 \cdot 2| = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{1} - 1 + C$ $\Rightarrow \ln|2| = \frac{1}{2} + C \Rightarrow C = \ln|2| - \frac{1}{2}$ From, Eq. (i), we get $\ln|x^2 y| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x + \ln|2| - \frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \ln|x^2 y| - \ln|2| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x - \frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \ln\left|\frac{1}{2} x^2 y\right| = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{x} - x - \frac{1}{2}$ which matches option (2). © examsnet.com

question: The general solution of the differential equation $\;\frac{dy}{dx}=\;\frac{2x+y-3}{2y-x+3}$ is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, differential equation $\;\frac{dy}{dx}=\;\frac{2x+y-3}{2y-x+3}$ Let $x=X+h, y=Y+k$ , then $\;\frac{dY}{dX}\;=\;\frac{2(X+h)+(Y+k)-3}{2(Y+k)-(X+h)+3}$ $\;=\;\frac{2X+Y+2h+k-3}{2Y-X+2k-h+3}$ Let $2h+k-3=0$ and $-h+2k+3=0$ Solving these two equations, we get $h=\;\frac{9}{5}$ and $k=\;\frac{-3}{5}$ So, Eq. (i) becomes, $\;\frac{dY}{dX}=\;\frac{2X+Y}{2Y-X}$ Let $Y=vX$ $\Rightarrow \;\frac{dY}{dX}=v+X \;\frac{dv}{dX'}$ Substituting this into Eq. (ii), we get $\Rightarrow \;\;  x \;\frac{dv}{dx}\;=\;\frac{2+v}{2v-1}-v$ $\;\Rightarrow \;\frac{2+v-2v^2+v}{2v-1}$ $\;=\;\frac{2v-2v^2+2}{2v-1}$ $\Rightarrow \;\frac{2v-1}{-2v^2+2v+2} dv=\;\frac{2+v}{2v-1}$ Integrating both sides, we get $\int\;\frac{2v-1}{-2v^2+2v+2} dv=\int\;\frac{dX}{X}$ Let $u=-2v^2+2v+2$ Then $du=(-4v+2)dv$ $\therefore \;\frac{-1}{2} \int\;\frac{du}{u}=\int\;\frac{dX}{X} \Rightarrow \;\frac{-1}{2} \ln \lvert u \rvert = \ln \lvert X \rvert + c_1,$ where $c_1=$ constant $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \;\frac{-1}{2} \ln \lvert -2v^2+2v+2 \rvert =\ln \lvert X \rvert +c_1$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \ln \lvert -2v^2+2v+2 \rvert =-2 \ln \lvert X \rvert +c_2$ where $c_2=-2c_1$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  \ln \lvert X^2 (-2v^2+2v+2) \rvert =c_2$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  X^2 (-2v^2+2v+2) =c, \;\text{ where }\; c=e^{c_2}$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  X^2 \left( \;\frac{-2Y^2}{X^2}+\;\frac{2Y}{X}+2 \right) =c$ $\;\Rightarrow  \;\;  (-2Y^2+2XY+2X^2) =c$ Substitute $X$ and $Y$ , we get $\;-2\left(y+\;\frac{3}{5}\right)^2+2\left(x-\;\frac{9}{5}\right)\left(y+\;\frac{3}{5}\right)+2\left(x-\;\frac{9}{5}\right)^2=c$ $\;\Rightarrow-2\left(y^2+\;\frac{6}{5}y+\;\frac{9}{25}\right)+2\left(xy+\;\frac{3}{5}x-\;\frac{9}{5}y-\;\frac{27}{25}\right)+2\left(x^2-\;\frac{18}{5}x+\;\frac{81}{25}\right)=c$ $\; \;\;  \Rightarrow  \;\; -2y^2-\;\frac{12}{5}y-\;\frac{18}{25}+2xy+\;\frac{6}{5}x-\;\frac{18}{5}y$ $\; \;\; -\;\frac{54}{25}+2x^2-\;\frac{36}{5}x+\;\frac{162}{25}=c$ $\;\Rightarrow-2y^2+2xy+2x^2-\;\frac{30}{5}y-\;\frac{30}{5}x+\;\frac{90}{25}=c$ $\;\Rightarrow 2x^2+2xy-2y^2-6x-6y=c$ $\;\Rightarrow x^2+xy-y^2-3x-3y=c$ Thus, the general solution is $x^2+xy-y^2-3x-3y+c=0$ © examsnet.com

question: If $x \log x \;\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\log x^2$ and $y(e)=0$ , then $y(e^2)=$ [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given, $x \log x \;\frac{dy}{dx}+y=\log x^2$ $y(e)=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x \log x}y=\frac{\log x^2}{x \log x}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x \log x}y=\frac{2 \log x}{x \log x}=\frac{2}{x}$ This is a linear differential equation of the form $\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)$ , Where $P(x)=\frac{1}{x \log x}$ and $Q(x)=\frac{2}{x}$ Now, $IF = e^{\int \frac{1}{x \log x} dx}$ Let $u=\log x$ . Then $du = \frac{1}{x} dx$ So, $IF = e^{\int \frac{1}{u} du} = e^{\log u} = u = \log x$ So, the solution is given by $y \cdot IF = \int Q(x) \cdot IF dx + c$ $y \log x = \int \frac{2}{x} \log x dx + c$ Let $v=\log x$ Then, $dv = \frac{1}{x} dx$ $\text{So,}\; y \log x = \int 2v dv + c = v^2 + c$ $\Rightarrow y \log x = v^2 + c = (\log x)^2 + c$ Given, $y(e)=0$ So, $y \log x = (\log x)^2 + c$ $\Rightarrow 0 \cdot \log(e) = (\log e)^2 + c$ $\Rightarrow 0 = 1 + c \Rightarrow c = -1$ ∴ The particular solution is $y \log x = (\log x)^2 - 1$ $\Rightarrow y = \frac{(\log x)^2 - 1}{\log x}$ So, $y(e^2) = \frac{(\log e^2)^2 - 1}{\log(e^2)}$ $= \frac{(2 \log e)^2 - 1}{2 \log(e)} \quad [\because \log e = 1]$ $= \frac{2^2 - 1}{2} = \frac{4 - 1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}$ $\therefore y(e^2) = \frac{3}{2}$ © examsnet.com

question: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration and its velocity at a time of ' $n$ ' seconds is ' v '. The total displacement of the body in the $n^{\;\text{th }\;}$ and $(n-1)^{\;\text{th }\;}$ seconds of its motion is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Step 1: Find acceleration $a$ . We use the formula for velocity with uniform acceleration: $v=u+at$ . Here, $u=0$ (because the body starts from rest), and after $n$ seconds, the velocity is $v$ . So: $v=an \Rightarrow a = \; \frac{v}{n}$ Step 2: Find displacement in the $n$ th second $(S_n)$ . The formula for how far an object moves during the $n$ th second is: $S_n = u + \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-1)$ Since $u=0$ : $S_n = \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-1)$ Step 3: Find displacement in the $(n-1)$ th second $(S_{n-1})$ . Plug ( $n-1$ ) instead of $n$ into the formula: $S_{n-1} \; = \; \frac{a}{2} (2(n-1)-1)$ $\; = \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-3)$ Step 4: Add the displacements for the $n$ th and $(n-1)$ th seconds. $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-1) + \; \frac{a}{2} (2n-3)$ Combine the numbers in the brackets: $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{a}{2} [(2n-1)+(2n-3)] = \; \frac{a}{2} (4n-4)$ Step 5: Substitute $a = \; \frac{v}{n}$ from Step 1. $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{1}{2} \cdot \; \frac{v}{n} \cdot (4n-4) = \; \frac{v}{2n} (4n-4)$ Simplify: $S_n + S_{n-1} = \; \frac{v}{2n} \cdot 4(n-1) = \; \frac{2v}{n} (n-1)$ © examsnet.com

question: If the range of a body projected with a velocity of $60\ \mathrm{m}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ is $180\sqrt{3}\ \mathrm{m}$ , then the angle of projection of the body is (Acceleration due to gravity $=10\ \mathrm{m}\ \mathrm{s}^{-2}$ ) [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Step 1: Write the formula for range The formula to find the range $R$ when a body is projected is: $R = \frac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$ Step 2: Put in the given values Here, $R = 180\sqrt{3}\ \mathrm{m},\ u = 60\ \mathrm{m/s}$ , and $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ . Step 3: Arrange the formula to find $\sin 2\theta$ $\sin 2\theta = \frac{R g}{u^2}$ Step 4: Substitute the values $\sin 2\theta = \frac{180\sqrt{3} \times 10}{60 \times 60}$ $\sin 2\theta = \frac{1800\sqrt{3}}{3600} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ Step 5: Identify the angle for $\sin 2\theta$ We know that $\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ . So, $2\theta = 60^{\circ}$ $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ Step 6: Check for other possible angles The range at angle $\theta$ is the same as at $90^{\circ} - \theta$ . So, the angle of projection can be $30^{\circ}$ or $60^{\circ}$ . © examsnet.com

question: If a force $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\,\text{N}$ acting on a body displaces it from point $(1\,\text{m}, 2\,\text{m})$ to point ( $2\,\text{m}, 0\,\text{m}$ ), then work done by the force is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Displacement vector of the body is $\vec{S} = (x_2 - x_1)\hat{i} + (y_2 - y_1)\hat{j}$ $= (2-1)\hat{i} + (0-2)\hat{j}$ $= \hat{i} - 2\hat{j}\ \text{m}$ Force acting on the body is $\vec{F} = (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})\ \text{N}$ Work done, $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{S}$ $= (3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j}) \cdot (\hat{i} - 2\hat{j})$ $= (3)(1) + (-2)(-2)$ $= 3 + 4 = 7\ \text{J}$ Hence, the work done by the force is $7\ \text{J}$ . © examsnet.com

question: A body moving along a straight line collides another body of same mass moving in the same direction with half of the velocity of the first body. If the coefficient of restitution between the two bodies is 0.5 , then the ratio of the velocities of the two bodies after collision is (treat the collision as one dimensional) [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Let initial velocities are $u$ and $\; \frac{u}{2}$ and final velocities are $v_A$ and $v_B$ . Then, momentum is conserved, $m u + \frac{m u}{2} = m v_A + m v_B$ or $v_A + v_B = \frac{3 u}{2}$ Coefficient of restitution is 0.5 , $\Rightarrow e = \frac{v_B - v_A}{u_A - u_B} = \frac{v_B - v_A}{u - \left(\frac{u}{2}\right)}$ $\Rightarrow v_B - v_A = \frac{u}{4} \ldots (ii)$ From (i) and (ii) $v_B = \frac{7}{8} \cdot u$ And from (i) and (iii) $v_A = \frac{5}{8} u$ Hence, ratio $\frac{v_A}{v_B} = \frac{\frac{5}{8}}{\frac{7}{8}} = \frac{5}{7}$ © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: As sphere is in pure rolling, $v=R\omega$ Rotational KE of sphere $=\frac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ $=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{5}mR^2\omega^2=\frac{1}{5}mv^2$ Kinetic energy of translation $=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ Total $KE = \left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{5}\right)mv^2=\frac{7}{10}mv^2$ Required ratio $=\frac{1}{5}\times\frac{10}{7}=\frac{2}{7}$ © examsnet.com

question: The time period of a simple pendulum on the surface of the earth is T . If the pendulum is taken to a height equal to half of the radius of the earth, then its time period is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Time period of a simple pendulum on the surface of the earth is $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$ At a height $h = \frac{R}{2}$ above the earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is $g_h = g \left( \frac{R}{R+h} \right)^2 = g \left( \frac{R}{R + \frac{R}{2}} \right)^2 = g \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^2 = \frac{4}{9} g$ So the time period at that height becomes $T' = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g_h}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\frac{4}{9} g}} = \frac{3}{2} \left( 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{g}} \right)$ $\therefore T' = \frac{3}{2} T$ Hence the correct option is $\frac{3T}{2}$ . © examsnet.com

subject: Physics
question: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion starting from its mean position. If the time period of the particle is 1.5 s , then the minimum time at which the ratio of the kinetic and total energies of the particle becomes $3 : 4$ is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: For particle in SHM, $T = 1.5\ \mathrm{sso}$ $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{4\pi}{3}\ \mathrm{rad/s}$ Let oscillations starts from $t = 0$ and $x = A \sin \omega t$ is displacement equation Then, KE at time $t$ is, $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m \left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{2} m \cdot A^{2} \omega^{2} \cos^{2} \omega t \cdots (i)$ And total energy of particle is, $E = \frac{1}{2} k A^{2}$ Here, $k = m \omega^{2}$ $= \frac{1}{2} m A^{2} \omega^{2} \cdots (ii)$ Given, ratio, $\frac{K}{E} = \frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \frac{ \frac{1}{2} m A^{2} \omega^{2} \cos^{2} \omega t }{ \frac{1}{2} m A^{2} \omega^{2} } = \frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \cos^{2} \omega t = \frac{3}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \cos \omega t = \sqrt{ \frac{3}{2} }$ $\Rightarrow \omega t = \frac{\pi}{6}$ $\Rightarrow t = \frac{\pi}{6\omega} = \frac{\pi \times 3}{6 \times 4\pi} = \frac{1}{8}\ \mathrm{s}$ © examsnet.com

subject: Physics
question: If the escape velocity of a body from the surface of the earth is $11.2\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ , then the orbital velocity of a satellite in an orbit which is at a height equal to the radius of the earth is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Step 1: Escape velocity from the Earth's surface $v_{\text{escape}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = 11.2\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ Here $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass of the Earth and $R$ is the radius of the Earth. Step 2: Orbital velocity of a satellite at height $h = R$ The orbital velocity at a distance $r$ from the centre of the Earth is $v_{\text{orbit}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$ . For a height $h = R$ , the orbital radius is $r = R + R = 2R$ . So $v_{\text{orbit}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}}$ . Step 3: Compare the two velocities $\frac{v_{\text{orbit}}}{v_{\text{escape}}} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}}}{\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{2R}\cdot\frac{R}{2GM}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$ Hence the orbital velocity is half the escape velocity. Step 4: Substitute the given value $v_{\text{orbit}} = \frac{v_{\text{escape}}}{2} = \frac{11.2}{2} = 5.6\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ Therefore the correct option is $5.6\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . © examsnet.com

question: A wire is stretched 1 mm by a force F . If a second wire of same material, same length and 4 times the diameter of the first wire is stretched by the same force $F$ , then the elongation of the second wire is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Step 1: Formula for Elongation The amount a wire stretches depends on Young's modulus formula: $Y=\;\frac{F l}{\Delta l A}=\;\frac{4 F l}{\Delta l \pi d^2}$ Step 2: What stays the same? Both wires are made of the same material, have the same length, and the same stretching force. This means their Young's modulus $(Y)$ , original length $(l)$ , and force $(F)$ are the same. Step 3: Setting up the equation for both wires Since Young's modulus is the same for both wires, we set the formulas equal for each wire: $Y_1=Y_2$ $\;\frac{4 F l}{\Delta l_1 \pi d_1^2}=\;\frac{4 F l}{\Delta l_2 \pi d_2^2}$ Step 4: Rearranging to compare elongations We can simplify to find how the elongation ( $\Delta l$ ) relates to diameter ( $d$ ): $\Delta l_1 \cdot d_1^2 = \Delta l_2 \cdot d_2^2$ So, $\Delta l_2 = \Delta l_1 \cdot \left( \;\frac{d_1}{d_2} \right)^2$ Step 5: Substitute values We are told $\Delta l_1 = 1\,\text{mm}$ (the first wire stretches 1 mm ) and $d_2 = 4 d_1$ (the second wire's diameter is 4 times bigger). $\Delta l_2 = 1 \cdot \left( \;\frac{d_1}{4 d_1} \right)^2 = 1 \cdot \left( \;\frac{1}{4} \right)^2 = \;\frac{1}{16} \text{mm}$ Final Answer The second, thicker wire stretches only $\;\frac{1}{16} \text{mm}$ when the same force is applied. © examsnet.com

question: A refrigerator of coefficient of performance 5 that extracts heat from the cooling compartment at the rate of 250 J per cycle is placed in a room. The heat released per cycle to the room by the refrigerator is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

solution: Solution: Step 1: For a refrigerator, the coefficient of performance is defined as the heat extracted from the cold compartment divided by the work input per cycle: $COP = \frac{Q_C}{W}$ Step 2: Here $COP = 5$ and $Q_C = 250 \, \text{J}$ , so the work done per cycle is: $W = \frac{Q_C}{COP} = \frac{250}{5} = 50 \, \text{J}$ Step 3: By conservation of energy (first law) for one cycle, the heat rejected to the room equals the heat absorbed from the cooling compartment plus the work input: $Q_H = Q_C + W$ Step 4: Substitute the values: $Q_H = 250 \, \text{J} + 50 \, \text{J} = 300 \, \text{J}$ Step 5: Hence the heat released per cycle to the room is $300 \, \text{J}$ , which matches the option $300 \, \text{J}$ . © examsnet.com

question: Two charged particles of specific charges in the ratio $2: 1$ and masses in the ratio $1: 4$ moving with same kinetic energy enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles to the direction of the field. answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: For a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field, the radius of the circular path is $r=\frac{mv}{Bq}$ Since kinetic energy is $K=\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ , we have $mv=\sqrt{2mK}$ , so $r=\frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{Bq}$ Writing charge in terms of the specific charge $s=\frac{q}{m}$ (so $q=ms$ ), $r=\frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{B\,m\,s}=\frac{\sqrt{2K}}{B\,s\sqrt{m}}$ Thus $r\propto \frac{1}{s\sqrt{m}}$ for the same $K$ and $B$ . Given $s_1:s_2=2:1$ and $m_1:m_2=1:4$ , $\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\frac{s_2}{s_1}\sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{s_2}{s_1}\right)^2\left(\frac{m_2}{m_1}\right)}$ $\frac{r_1}{r_2}=\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{4}{1}\right)}=\sqrt{1}=1$ Hence $r_1:r_2=1:1$ . Correct option: $1:1$ © examsnet.com

subject: Physics
question: A sample of paramagnetic salt contains $2 \times 10^{24}$ atomic dipoles each of dipole moment $1.5 \times 10^{-23} \text{JT}^{-1}$ . The sample is placed under homogeneous magnetic field of 0.6 T and cooled to a temperature 4.2 K . The degree of magnetic saturation achived is $20\%$ . Then total dipole moment of the sample for a magnetic field of 0.9 T and a temperature of 2.8 K is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: We use Curie's law to understand how the magnetism of a paramagnetic material changes with temperature and magnetic field. According to Curie's law, the magnetisation $(M)$ is directly proportional to the magnetic field $(B_0)$ and inversely proportional to the temperature $(T)$ : $M \propto \frac{B_0}{T}$ or, $M = C \cdot \frac{B_0}{T}$ where $C$ (Curie's constant) stays the same for the same substance. Curie's constant can be written as: $C = \frac{M T}{B_0}$ where: $T =$ temperature in Kelvin $B_0 =$ external magnetic field $M =$ magnetisation (total dipole moment) Since $C$ (Curie's constant) is the same for all measurements of the same sample, we can relate two cases as: $\frac{M_1 T_1}{B_{0_1}} = \frac{M_2 T_2}{B_{0_2}}$ So, $M_2 = M_1 \cdot \frac{T_1}{T_2} \cdot \frac{B_{0_2}}{B_{0_1}}$ Now, let's fill in the given values: Number of dipoles $= 2 \times 10^{24}$ Dipole moment per dipole $= 15 \times 10^{-23} \text{JT}^{-1}$ Step 1: Find Initial Total Dipole Moment Total dipole moment possible (if $100\%$ aligned): $2 \times 10^{24} \times 15 \times 10^{-23} = 3 \times 10^2 \text{JT}^{-1}$ But, at first, only $20\%$ saturation is achieved: $M_1 = 0.2 \times 3 \times 10^2 = 60 \text{JT}^{-1}$ Step 2: Use Curie's Law for New Conditions Magnetic field changes from $B_{0_1} = 0.6 \text{T}$ to $B_{0_2} = 0.9 \text{T}$ and temperature from $T_1 = 4.2 \text{K}$ to $T_2 = 2.8 \text{K}$ . Now, use the formula: $M_2 = M_1 \times \frac{T_1}{T_2} \times \frac{B_{0_2}}{B_{0_1}}$ Substitute the numbers in: $M_2 = 60 \times \frac{4.2}{2.8} \times \frac{0.9}{0.6}$ Calculate step by step: $\frac{4.2}{2.8} = 1.5$ $\frac{0.9}{0.6} = 1.5$ So, $M_2 = 60 \times 1.5 \times 1.5 = 135 \text{JT}^{-1}$ © examsnet.com

question: A coil of resistance $200 \Omega$ is placed in a magnetic field. If the magnetic flux $\phi$ (in weber) linked with the coil varies with time ' $t$ ' (in second) as per the equation $\phi=50 t^2+4$ , then the current induced in the coil at a time $t=2\,\mathrm{s}$ is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

solution: Solution: We need to find the current in the coil at $t=2$ seconds. Step 1: Find the induced EMF. The magnetic flux is given by $\phi=50 t^2+4$ . To find the EMF ( $E$ ), we take the derivative of $\phi$ with respect to $t$ : $E=\;\frac{d\phi}{dt}$ Now, differentiate $\phi$ : $\;\frac{d}{dt} (50 t^2+4) =100 t$ (because the derivative of $t^2$ is $2t$ , and 50 times $2t$ is $100t$ ; the derivative of a constant is 0 ). Step 2: Calculate EMF at $t=2$ seconds. Plug in $t=2$ : $E=100 \times 2=200\;\text{ volts }\;$ Step 3: Find the current using Ohm's Law. Ohm's Law: $I=\;\frac{E}{R}$ Here, $E=200$ volts and $R=200 \Omega$ . $I=\;\frac{200}{200}=1\ \mathrm{A}$ So, the current induced in the coil at $t=2$ seconds is 1 ampere. © examsnet.com

question: A laser produces a beam of light of frequency $5 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ with an output power of 33 mW . The average number of photons emitted by the laser per second is $($ Planck's constant $= 6.6 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J} \text{ s})$ [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

solution: Solution: Step 1: Understanding Power Power is how much energy is used or given out each second. subject: Chemistry
question: Consider the following Statement-I $\; :$ Both $\mathrm{BeSO}_4$ and $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ are readily soluble in water. Statement-II : Among the nitrates of alkaline earth metals, only $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ on strong heating gives its oxide, $\mathrm{NO}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ . The correct answer is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

options.A: Both Statement-I and statement-II are correct
options.B: Statement-I is correct, but statement-II is not correct
options.C: Statement-I is not correct, but statement-II is correct
options.D: Both statement-I and statement-II are not correct

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Analysis of Statement-I: Both $\mathrm{BeSO}_4$ and $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ are readily soluble in water. The solubility of sulfates of alkaline earth metals generally decreases down the group. $\mathrm{BeSO}_4$ (Beryllium sulfate) is readily soluble in water. This is due to the very small size of the $\mathrm{Be}^{2+}$ ion, which leads to very high hydration energy. This high hydration energy more than compensates for the relatively high lattice energy, making it highly soluble. $\mathrm{MgSO}_4$ (Magnesium sulfate, commonly known as Epsom salt) is also readily soluble in water. Similar to beryllium, the $\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}$ ion is relatively small, leading to significant hydration energy. In contrast, $\mathrm{CaSO}_4$ (Calcium sulfate) is sparingly soluble, and $\mathrm{SrSO}_4$ (Strontium sulfate) and $\mathrm{BaSO}_4$ (Barium sulfate) are practically insoluble. Therefore, Statement - I is correct. Analysis of Statement - II: Among the nitrates of alkaline earth metals, only $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ on strong heating gives its oxide, $\mathrm{NO}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ . Alkaline earth metal nitrates decompose on strong heating to give the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide ( $\mathrm{NO}_2$ ), and oxygen $(\mathrm{O}_2)$ . The general reaction is: $2 \mathrm{M}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2(s) \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} 2 \mathrm{MO}(s) + 4 \mathrm{NO}_2(g) + \mathrm{O}_2(g)$ This decomposition pattern is observed for all alkaline earth metal nitrates. $\; \mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} \mathrm{BeO} + 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2$ $\; \mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} \mathrm{MgO} + 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2$ $\; \mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\; \text{heat} \;} \mathrm{CaO} + 2 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2$ And similarly for $\mathrm{Sr}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ and $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ . The thermal stability of these nitrates generally increases down the group $(\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2.$ is the least stable, and $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ is the most stable), meaning they decompose at different temperatures, but the decomposition products are the same for all of them. The statement claims that "only $\mathrm{Be}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_2$ " decomposes in this manner, which is incorrect as all alkaline earth metal nitrates follow this decomposition pathway. Therefore, Statement - II is not correct. Conclusion: Statement - I is correct. Statement - II is not correct. This matches option B. © examsnet.com

question: Which one of the following statements related to photochemical smog is not correct? [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

options.A: It is controlled by the use of catalytic converters in automobiles
options.C: It is a mixture of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ , smoke and fog
options.D: It causes extensive damage to plant life

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Photochemical smog: Formed when sunlight acts on nitrogen oxides (NOx) and hydrocarbons (unburnt fuel), producing secondary pollutants like ozone $(\mathrm{O}_3)$ , peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), formaldehyde, etc. It is also called Los Angeles smog or summer smog. It mainly occurs in warm, dry, and sunny climates. Option A: It is controlled by the use of catalytic converters in automobiles. Correct. Catalytic converters reduce emissions of NOx and hydrocarbons, which are precursors of photochemical smog. Option B: It causes corrosion of metals. Correct. Ozone and other oxidants in photochemical smog can corrode metals. Option C: It is a mixture of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ , smoke, and fog. Not correct. This describes classical smog (also called London smog or reducing smog), which occurs in cool, humid conditions and is a mixture of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ and particulates with fog. Photochemical smog, on the other hand, contains NOx, hydrocarbons, and oxidants such as ozone-not SO2-based smoke and fog. Option D: It causes extensive damage to plant life. Correct. Ozone and PAN damage leaves and affect photosynthesis. © examsnet.com

question: An element occurs in the body centred cubic structure with edge length of 288 pm . The density of the element is $7.2\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ . The number of atoms present in 208 g of the element is nearly [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Given Values: The edge length $a=288\ \mathrm{pm}$ . The density $(\rho)$ is $7.2\ \mathrm{g}/\mathrm{cm}^3$ . The mass given is 208 g . Step 1: Find volume of one unit cell The edge length must be changed to centimeters: $1\ \mathrm{pm}=10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}$ . So: $a=288 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}$ . The volume of one unit cell is: $V=a^3= (288 \times 10^{-10})^3\ \mathrm{cm}^3=2.389 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ Step 2: Find total volume that 208 g will occupy $V_{\text{total}} = \frac{m}{\rho} = \frac{208}{7.2} = 28.89\ \mathrm{cm}^3$ Step 3: Find the number of unit cells in $208\ \mathrm{g}$ $\text{Number of unit cells} = \frac{V_{\text{total}}}{V_{\text{unit cell}}} = \frac{28.89}{2.389 \times 10^{-23}} = 1.209 \times 10^{24}$ Step 4: Find the total number of atoms A body centered cubic (bcc) unit cell has 2 atoms per unit cell. So, Total atoms $=$ Number of unit cells $\times 2=1.209 \times 10^{24} \times 2=2.42 \times 10^{24}$ which is the same as $24.2 \times 10^{23}$ . © examsnet.com

question: An aqueous solution containing 0.2 g of a non volatile solute ' A ' in 21.5 g of water freezes at 272.814 K . If the freezing point of water is 273.16 K , the molar mass (in $\mathrm{g} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ ) of solute $A$ is $[ K_f (\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}) = 1.86 \mathrm{K} \mathrm{kg} \mathrm{mol}^{-1} ]$ [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Step 1: Find the decrease in freezing point The difference between the normal freezing point of water and the solution's freezing point is called the depression in freezing point. The calculation is: $\; \Delta T_f = T_f^0 - T_f = 273.16 - 272.814$ $\; \Delta T_f = 0.346 \mathrm{K}$ Step 2: Use the freezing point depression formula The formula is: $\Delta T_f = K_f \cdot m$ where $m$ is molality. $m = \; \frac{\Delta T_f}{K_f} = \; \frac{0.346}{1.86} = 0.186 \mathrm{mol/kg}$ Step 3: Calculate the moles of solute Molality tells us moles of solute in 1 kg of solvent (water). Here, amount of water is $21.5 \mathrm{g} = 0.0215 \mathrm{kg}$ . Moles of solute $= 0.186 \times 0.0215 = 0.00400 \mathrm{mol}$ Step 4: Calculate the molar mass Molar mass $= \frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{moles of solute}}$ Molar mass $= \frac{0.2}{0.00400} = 50 \mathrm{g/mol}$ © examsnet.com

question: What is the indicator used in Argentometric titrations? [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Argentometric titrations are titrations involving silver nitrate $(\mathrm{AgNO}_3)$ as the titrant, typically used for the determination of halide ions such as $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}, \mathrm{Br}^{-}$ , and $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ . One common method is the Fajans method, where an adsorption indicator, such as fluorescein or eosin, is used. Before the equivalence point, halide ions are present in excess, and the precipitate surface $(\mathrm{AgX})$ is negatively charged. After the equivalence point, excess $\mathrm{Ag}^{+}$ ions make the surface positively charged, allowing the negatively charged dye ions (like eosin) to adsorb on the surface and cause a visible color change - signaling the end point. Hence, Eosin dye (an adsorption indicator) is used in argentometric titrations by Fajans' method. © examsnet.com

subject: Chemistry
question: The co-ordination number of chromium in $\mathrm{K} [ \mathrm{Cr} ( \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} )_2 ( \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4 )_2 ]$ is [AP EAPCET 24 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: To determine the coordination number of chromium $( \mathrm{Cr} )$ in the complex $\mathrm{K} [ \mathrm{Cr} ( \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} )_2 ( \mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4 )_2 ]$ , we need to identify the ligands and their denticity. Identify the central metal atom: The central metal atom is Chromium (Cr). Identify the ligands: $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ (aqua) $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4$ (oxalato, derived from oxalic acid, $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-}$ ) Determine the denticity of each ligand: $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ (water): This is a monodentate ligand, meaning each water molecule forms one coordinate bond with the central metal atom. $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-}$ (oxalate): This is a bidentate ligand, meaning each oxalate ion forms two coordinate bonds with the central metal atom, typically through its two oxygen atoms. Calculate the total number of coordinate bonds: There are two $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ ligands. Since each is monodentate, they contribute $2 \times 1 = 2$ coordinate bonds. There are two $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-}$ ligands. Since each is bidentate, they contribute $2 \times 2 = 4$ coordinate bonds. Sum the coordinate bonds to find the coordination number: Coordination number $= (.$ bonds from $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} ) + (.$ bonds from $\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4^{2-})$ Coordination number $=2+4=6$ Therefore, the coordination number of chromium in the given complex is 6 . The final answer is 6 . © examsnet.com

solution: Solution: Amylose: Amylose is a linear polymer made up of D-glucose units. The glucose units are linked together by $\alpha - 1 , 4$ -glycosidic bonds. Branching occurs due to $\alpha - 1 , 6$ -glycosidic bonds at intervals. Cellulose: Cellulose is a linear polymer of D-glucose units. The glucose units are linked by $\beta$ -1,4-glycosidic bonds. This type of linkage gives cellulose its rigid, structural properties. Now, let's match List-I (Glycosidic linkage) with List-II (Polysaccharide): (A) $\alpha - 1 , 4$ : This linkage is characteristic of the linear chains in both amylose and amylopectin. Since amylose only has $\alpha-1,4$ linkages for its main structure, it's the most direct match here. So, A - (I) Amylose. (B) $\beta$ -1,4: This linkage is unique to (III) Cellulose among the given options. So, B - (III) Cellulose. (C) $\alpha - 1 , 4 , \alpha - 1 , 6$ : The presence of both $\alpha -1,4$ and $\alpha -1,6$ linkages indicates a branched polysaccharide with alpha linkages, which is characteristic of (II) Amylopectin. solution: Solution: Let $A$ be the event that candidate A gets the job and $B$ be the event that candidate B gets the job. It is given that $P(A)=0.8$ and $P(B)=0.7$ . Assuming the selections are independent, $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)=0.8\times 0.7=0.56$ . The probability that at least one of them gets the job is $P(A\cup B)$ . By the addition theorem, $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$ . Thus, $P(A\cup B)=0.8+0.7-0.56=0.94$ . Hence, the correct answer is $0.94$ . © examsnet.com

subject: Chemistry
question: An alcohol $X(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{12}\mathrm{O})$ on dehydration gives Y (major product). Reaction of Y with HBr gave $Z(\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{11}\mathrm{Br}.)$ , major product). Z undergoes nucleophilic substitution in two steps. What are X and Y ? [AP EAPCET 26 May 2025 S1]

answer_provenance.method: single green option label (RGB 0,128,0); four option labels required

solution: Solution: Identify Z: Since Z undergoes nucleophilic substitution in two steps, it follows an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ mechanism, so Z must be a tertiary alkyl bromide. For the formula $\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{11}\mathrm{Br}$ , the tertiary bromide is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(Br)CH_2CH_3}$ . Identify Y: HBr addition to Y gives this tertiary bromide by Markovnikov addition, so Y is 2-methylbut-2-ene, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CHCH_3}$ . Identify X: Dehydration of X must give 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product. The alcohol that directly gives this more substituted alkene is 2-methylbutan-2-ol, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(OH)CH_2CH_3}$ . Mechanism check: Z ionizes slowly to a tertiary carbocation and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ , then the nucleophile attacks in a fast second step, confirming two-step $\mathrm{S_N1}$ substitution. Thus X is 2-methylbutan-2-ol and Y is 2-methylbut-2-ene, which corresponds to option option B. © examsnet.com
